opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a really nice connection there. One of the things that always attracted me to diffusion models is that they give you a very natural way to trade off compute for quality at inference time. You start from noise and you iteratively refine, and the number of refinement steps is something you can dial up or down. If you're willing to spend more compute, you take more steps, you correct more mistakes, and you generally get better samples. So the model isn't forced to commit to an answer in a single shot.

That's essentially the same intuition behind the excitement around chain of thought and test-time compute in LLMs. People realized that if you let the model "think" longer, generate intermediate reasoning, maybe revise itself, you can get much better answers on hard problems without changing the weights. You're scaling compute at inference rather than only at training.

The difference is how that extra compute gets spent. In an autoregressive model, the only way to think more is to emit more tokens, left to right, and once a token is written it's essentially fixed. So you get a lot of serial computation, and errors early in the chain can propagate. With diffusion, the refinement happens over the whole output in parallel. At every step the model can look at the entire sequence and fix things anywhere, not just at the end. That's a more global, coarse-to-fine kind of reasoning, and it's also much more parallelizable on modern hardware, which is one reason diffusion language models can be a lot faster.

So I see diffusion as a different, and in some ways more flexible, axis for test-time scaling. You can combine the two as well. You can imagine reasoning traces that are themselves generated and refined with diffusion, or using more denoising steps for harder problems and fewer for easy ones. I think we're just starting to explore that design space, and the fact that the community is now so focused on inference-time compute makes the diffusion perspective feel very timely.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there's actually a very deep connection there, and it's one of the things that got me excited about diffusion models in the first place. If you think about what a diffusion model does at inference time, it doesn't produce the output in one shot. It starts from noise and it iteratively refines its guess, step by step, until it converges on something that's coherent. So you're essentially spending compute at inference time to improve the quality of what you generate. The more steps you take, the better the sample tends to be, up to a point. And that's a knob you can turn. You can trade off latency for quality.

Now, chain of thought in language models is really the same idea in a different guise. Instead of the model committing to an answer immediately, you let it spend tokens, which is really just compute, working through intermediate steps before it produces the final answer. And empirically, the more of that reasoning you allow, the better the model does on hard problems. So in both cases, the key insight is that there's a lot of value in decoupling the amount of computation you spend at inference time from the amount you spent at training time. The traditional view was that a neural network is a fixed function, one forward pass, you get what you get. Diffusion models broke that for images, and chain of thought and the more recent reasoning models are breaking that for language.

The interesting difference, I'd say, is in how the refinement happens. In an autoregressive language model with chain of thought, the refinement is sequential and it's left to right. You generate a token, then the next one, and if you make a mistake early you kind of have to live with it or explicitly backtrack in words. In a diffusion model the refinement is global. Every step, you get to revise the entire output in parallel. You can fix something at the beginning based on what you've figured out at the end. And that's actually one of the motivations for the work we've been doing on diffusion language models. You get this planning-like behavior for free, because the model is looking at the whole sequence and iteratively improving it, rather than committing token by token. So I see chain of thought as a sort of validation of the broader principle, that inference-time compute matters a lot, and diffusion as a particularly natural and flexible way of implementing that principle, where the number of refinement steps becomes a first-class control that you can adjust depending on how hard the problem is.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a very interesting connection. With diffusion models, you don’t have to produce the answer in a single forward pass. You start with noise, and then you gradually refine it through a sequence of steps. So you have this opportunity to spend more computation at inference time to generate a better answer.

And that’s also part of the appeal of chain of thought. If you ask a language model a question and require it to answer immediately, you’re limiting how much computation it can do. If you allow it to generate intermediate steps, you’re giving it additional computation before it commits to an answer. For a difficult problem, that can be really valuable.

The mechanisms are different—diffusion steps aren’t necessarily reasoning steps—but the common idea is that intelligence shouldn’t have to happen in one fixed computational pass. You’d like to be able to spend more effort on harder problems. Of course, the challenge is making that extra computation useful: just taking more steps doesn’t automatically mean you’ll get a better answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a common intuition, which is that generating a good answer shouldn’t necessarily take a fixed amount of computation. If you ask a difficult question, you might want the model to spend more time working on it before committing to an answer.

Diffusion models give you a very explicit way of doing that. You start from noise and progressively refine a candidate through many steps. That was part of what I found appealing: generation becomes an iterative computational process, rather than a single forward pass.

With chains of thought, you see a related idea in language models. By producing intermediate tokens, the model gets additional computation before giving its final answer. The mechanisms are different—diffusion revises a representation, while an autoregressive model extends a sequence—but both raise this question of how to use computation at inference time to improve the result. And then the interesting challenge is making that extra computation productive, rather than simply taking more steps.
